title: Γυνὴ καὶ ἀνὴρ ⟨μέθυσος⟩
titleEn: The Woman and Her Drunkard Husband
part: The Woman and Her Drunkard Husband (Chambry 88 · Perry 246)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 88 (= Perry 246). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γυνή τις ἄνδρα μέθυσον εἶχε· τοῦ δὲ πάθους αὐτὸν ἀπαλλάξαι θέλουσα τοιόνδε τι σοφίζεται.
sentences.tr: Gynē tis andra methyson eiche· tou de pathous auton apallaxai thelousa toionde ti sophizetai.
sentences.l: A certain woman had a drunkard husband; and wishing to rid him of the affliction she contrives something of this kind.
sentences.n: ἀπαλλάξαι takes a genitive of separation, τοῦ πάθους, 'to release him from the affliction'. σοφίζεται is a historic present, dropped into the middle of past narrative to bring the scheme close. Note πάθος — the word returns in the last sentence, where it has become an ἕξις.

sentences.t: Κεκαρωμένον γὰρ αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τῆς μέθης παρατηρήσασα καὶ νεκροῦ δίκην ἀναισθητοῦντα ἐπ’ ὤμων ἄρασα ἐπὶ τὸ πολυάνδριον ἀπενεγκοῦσα κατέθετο καὶ ἀπῆλθεν.
sentences.tr: Kekarōmenon gar auton hypo tēs methēs paratērēsasa kai nekrou dikēn anaisthētounta ep’ ōmōn arasa epi to polyandrion apenenkousa katetheto kai apēlthen.
sentences.l: For having watched him stupefied by the drink and insensible after the manner of a corpse, having lifted him onto her shoulders, having carried him off to the common burial-ground, she laid him down and went away.
sentences.i: Watching until the drink had left him stupefied and as insensible as a corpse, she hoisted him onto her shoulders, carried him off to the common burial ground, laid him down there and left.
sentences.n: An aorist-participle chain — παρατηρήσασα, ἄρασα, ἀπενεγκοῦσα — with the finite verbs held back to the end: the engine of these fables, everything subordinate until the act that matters. δίκην with a genitive is adverbial, 'in the manner of'. τὸ πολυάνδριον is literally the place of many men, a public or common burial place.

sentences.t: Ἡνίκα δ’ αὐτὸν ἤδη ἀνανήφειν ἐστοχάσατο, προσελθοῦσα τὴν θύραν ἔκοπτε τοῦ πολυανδρίου.
sentences.tr: Hēnika d’ auton ēdē ananēphein estochasato, proselthousa tēn thyran ekopte tou polyandriou.
sentences.l: And when she reckoned that he was already sobering up, having come near she began knocking at the door of the burial-ground.
sentences.n: ἐστοχάσατο is 'aimed at, guessed' — a calculation, not knowledge; she is timing him. The πολυάνδριον is given a door here, so what the story pictures is a closed burial chamber rather than an open ground.

sentences.t: Ἐκείνου δὲ φήσαντος· « Τίς ὁ τὴν θύραν κόπτων ; » ἡ γυνὴ ἀπεκρίνατο· « Ὁ τοῖς νεκροῖς τὰ σιτία κομίζων ἐγὼ πάρειμι. »
sentences.tr: Ekeinou de phēsantos· « Tis ho tēn thyran koptōn ; » hē gynē apekrinato· « Ho tois nekrois ta sitia komizōn egō pareimi. »
sentences.l: And when he said: « Who is the one knocking at the door? » the woman answered: « I, the one who brings the dead their food, am here. »
sentences.n: Ἐκείνου δὲ φήσαντος, genitive absolute again. Food was in fact carried to the tomb as an offering for the dead, which is why the trick works: a voice at the door announcing provisions is exactly what a dead man would expect to hear.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος· « Μή μοι φαγεῖν, ἀλλὰ πιεῖν, ὦ βέλτιστε, μᾶλλον προσένεγκε· λυπεῖς γάρ με βρώσεως, ἀλλὰ μὴ πόσεως μνημονεύων. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinos· « Mē moi phagein, alla piein, ō beltiste, mallon prosenenke· lypeis gar me brōseōs, alla mē poseōs mnēmoneuōn. »
sentences.l: And he: « Not something to eat, but something to drink, my excellent fellow, bring me rather; for you grieve me by making mention of food and not of drink. »
sentences.i: And he answered: « Don't bring me something to eat, my good man — bring me something to drink; you pain me by talking of food and not of drink. »
sentences.n: No verb of speaking with Κἀκεῖνος: ἔφη is understood, a common economy in quick exchange. φαγεῖν and πιεῖν are aorist infinitives depending on προσένεγκε, and English has to supply a 'something' for them to hang on. ὦ βέλτιστε is masculine: from inside the tomb he takes the voice at the door for a man, and never recognises his wife.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ τὸ στῆθος πατάξασα· « Οἴμοι τῇ δυστήνῳ, φησίν· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὐδὲ σοφισαμένη ὤνησα· σὺ γάρ, ἄνερ, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἐπαιδεύθης, ἀλλὰ καὶ χείρων σαυτοῦ γέγονας, εἰς ἕξιν σοι καταστάντος τοῦ πάθους. »
sentences.tr: Hē de to stēthos pataxasa· « Oimoi tēi dystēnōi, phēsin· ouden gar oude sophisamenē ōnēsa· sy gar, aner, ou monon ouk epaideuthēs, alla kai cheirōn sautou gegonas, eis hexin soi katastantos tou pathous. »
sentences.l: And she, having struck her breast: « Alas for me, the wretched one, she says; for I did no good at all, not even by contriving; for you, husband, were not only not taught, but have even become worse than your own self, the affliction having settled into a fixed condition for you. »
sentences.i: And she beat her breast: « Wretched me! she says. All my contriving has done no good at all. You, husband, have not only not been taught your lesson — you have become worse than you were, now that the affliction has hardened into a settled habit. »
sentences.n: Οἴμοι takes a dative of the person lamented, here the speaker herself. ὤνησα is the active of ὀνίνημι, 'I benefited, did good', not the middle 'I profited': she is saying her scheme did no good, not that she gained nothing by it. χείρων σαυτοῦ, 'worse than your own self', a genitive of comparison turned against the man's earlier self. The closing phrase is a genitive absolute with a dative of interest: ἕξις is the term for a settled disposition — the πάθος of the first sentence has become permanent.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ταῖς κακαῖς πράξεσιν ἐγχρονίζειν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ou dei tais kakais praxesin enchronizein.
sentences.l: The fable shows that one must not linger in evil practices.
sentences.n: ἐγχρονίζω takes the dative, 'to spend time in' something.

sentences.t: Ἔστι γὰρ ὅτε καὶ μὴ θέλοντι τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ ἔθος ἐπιτίθεται.
sentences.tr: Esti gar hote kai mē thelonti tōi anthrōpōi to ethos epitithetai.
sentences.l: For there are times when the habit fastens upon a man even against his will.
sentences.n: ἔστιν ὅτε is a fixed phrase, literally 'there is when' = 'sometimes'. ἐπιτίθεμαι with the dative is the ordinary verb for a hostile assault: the habit attacks the man.
